common_name: Bride Eggplant (White and Purple-Streaked Asian Hybrid Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Bride is a compact, well-branching Asian type that sets clusters of two to three fruits per node rather than single large fruits.

directions: Bride is a Chinese-derived hybrid eggplant with slender, cylindrical fruit that emerges ivory-white and develops soft purple-lavender streaking as it fills out, topped by a distinctive green calyx. Fruit is best picked around 6-8 inches long and 1.5 inches thick, while the streaking is still light and the flesh is at its most tender and mild. The compact, branching plants set fruit in small clusters rather than singly, giving a steady succession of harvests through the hot part of the season. Because the thin skin bruises easily, handle fruit gently and cook it soon after picking in stir-fries or on the grill.

common_name: Shoya Long Eggplant (Japanese Hybrid Long Purple Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Shoya Long is an early, upright hybrid that suits both open-field summer plantings and season-extending tunnel culture in cooler climates.

directions: Shoya Long is a Japanese-type hybrid bred for exceptionally long, slender fruit with glossy deep-purple skin and a matching dark calyx, often reaching 14-16 inches with tender, nearly seedless flesh. The upright, vigorous plant habit keeps the long fruit off the ground and makes picking easier than with sprawling heirloom types. It matures early and yields heavily over a long harvest window, staying productive through the hottest stretch of a Gulf Coast summer. Harvest while the skin still has a bright sheen, since fruit left too long on the plant dulls and toughens.

common_name: Nubia Eggplant (Purple and White Variegated Italian-Type Hybrid Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Nubia matures somewhat later than many Italian hybrids, so give it the full length of a warm Gulf Coast season to size up properly.

directions: Nubia produces oval fruit boldly variegated in purple and white, growing 6-7 inches long and 3-4 inches across, with dense, cream-colored flesh and a mild, semi-sweet flavor. Because it fills out its fruit over a slightly longer window than many hybrids, keep plants evenly watered and well fed through the back half of summer rather than expecting an early flush. Slicing the flesh and salting it briefly before cooking helps draw out moisture and firms the texture for roasting, grilling, or caponata. Pick fruit while the variegated skin is still glossy, since it dulls noticeably once past peak ripeness.

common_name: De Barbentane Eggplant (Violette Longue de Barbentane, French Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; De Barbentane was selected in Provence for reliable cropping under cooler summer conditions, so it also finishes unusually early and productively in the long, hot Gulf Coast season.

directions: De Barbentane is a French heirloom dating to the early 1800s from the Provence region, prized for its shiny dark-purple, cylindrical fruit and firm, sweetly fragrant flesh with little of the bitterness common in older eggplant types. Vigorous plants routinely carry eight to ten fruits at once, each 6-8 inches long, making it one of the more heavily fruiting heirloom eggplants once established. Its early finish and cool-summer breeding background mean it sets fruit reliably even in a season that starts on the cool side. Harvest while the skin is still taut and glossy for the best flavor in ratatouille or grilled preparations.

common_name: Machiaw Eggplant (Asian Hybrid Long Pink-Purple Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Machiaw performed among the top Asian-type entries in a Midwest university eggplant trial and holds up well under hot, humid summer conditions.

directions: Machiaw is an Asian-type hybrid bearing slender fruit that ranges from pale purple to a striking deep pink, typically 10-12 inches long and about 1-1.5 inches thick. The skin stays thin and tender even as the fruit lengthens, giving mild, non-bitter flesh that needs no peeling or salting before cooking. Plants set fruit continuously through hot weather, making Machiaw a dependable choice for a long Gulf Coast harvest season. Pick fruit while the color is bright and the surface glossy, since the thin skin toughens and dulls quickly once fruit is left to over-mature.
sources: Purdue University Midwest Vegetable Variety Trial Report

common_name: Bambino Eggplant (Dwarf Container Mini Purple-Black Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Bambino's dwarf stature makes it one of the few eggplant types suited to large patio pots as well as garden beds.

directions: Bambino is a true dwarf eggplant, growing only 12-20 inches tall on plants with dark stems and lavender flowers, yet it sets heavy clusters of one to three small purple-black fruits at nearly every node. Its small stature and shallow root system make it a strong performer in containers, where its compact form fits tight patios and balconies as easily as a garden row. It begins fruiting earlier than most standard-sized eggplants and keeps producing steadily once established. Pick the egg-sized fruit while still glossy and firm, before the skin dulls and seeds inside begin to harden.

common_name: Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa Eggplant (Italian Heirloom Blushed White Egg-Shaped Eggplant)
scientific_name: Solanum melongena 'Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa'

planting.note: Start indoors 8 weeks before transplanting; this heirloom has a medium-late cycle, so give it the full length of a hot Gulf Coast summer to size up its large, egg-shaped fruit fully.

directions: Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa is an Italian heirloom producing large, rounded, egg-to-pear-shaped fruit 5-6 inches across, with creamy white skin that gradually takes on a soft lavender-pink blush as it ripens. The firm, creamy white flesh is sweet and free of the bitterness found in many older eggplant types, so it needs no pre-salting before cooking. Its classic rounded shape and thick flesh walls make it especially well suited to stuffing and baking whole, in addition to standard slicing preparations. Harvest as soon as the rosy blush develops fully across the skin, since fruit left on the vine longer turns fully rose-colored and the texture coarsens.
